summary: Describes a transport relay translator that lets IPv6-only hosts talk to IPv4 hosts by relaying TCP or UDP connections. It was an early transition technique.

plainLanguage.summary: A transport relay translator lets a computer that only speaks IPv6 reach a server that only speaks IPv4. It accepts the connection from the computer, opens a second connection to the server in IPv4, and passes the bytes between the two. Nothing has to be changed at either end, but the translator has to remember every connection it is carrying, and it cannot carry IPsec.

questions: what is a transport relay translator
subtitle: A middle system that carries IPv6 connections out to IPv4 servers without changing anything at either end.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only network still needs to reach IPv4-only resources outside it, such as IPv4-only web servers on the wider Internet.
tldr.mechanism: A transport relay translator sits in the middle and carries two connections instead of one: it accepts the IPv6 connection from the client and opens an IPv4 connection to the server, forwarding bytes between them. The client reaches the IPv4 server through an IPv6 address built from a reserved prefix and the server's IPv4 address.
tldr.outcome: Nothing at either end has to change, and the translator sidesteps path MTU problems. The cost is that it is stateful, acts as a single point of failure, and cannot carry IPsec. The memo is Informational.

facts.label: Reference implementation
facts.value: FAITH, in the WIDE KAME IPv6 stack

today: RFC 3142 is an Informational memo, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It describes a transport relay translator built from existing technologies and defines no new protocol. Its appendix records that the FAITH implementation, which does TRT for TCP, had been operational for more than five years and was used at IETF meetings to let more than 100 IPv6-only hosts reach IPv4 hosts. It is read with RFC 2765, the stateless translator it compares itself against.

sections.title: The Problem and the Proposal
sections.content:
When you deploy an IPv6-only network, you still want to gain access to IPv4-only network resources outside it, such as IPv4-only web servers. Many IPv6-to-IPv4 translation technologies have been proposed, mainly in the IETF ngtrans working group. The memo describes a translator based on the transport relay technique that solves the same problem, and calls it TRT, a transport relay translator. A TRT system locates between IPv6-only hosts and IPv4 hosts and translates {TCP,UDP}/IPv6 to {TCP,UDP}/IPv4, or vice versa.

The advantages are that TRT is designed to require no extra modification on IPv6-only initiating hosts, nor on IPv4-only destination hosts, whereas some other translation mechanisms need extra modifications on the initiating hosts, which limits the possibility of deployment. And the IPv6-to-IPv4 header converters have to take care of path MTU and fragmentation issues, while TRT is free from this problem.

The disadvantages are that TRT supports bidirectional traffic only, whereas the header converters may be able to support other cases such as unidirectional multicast datagrams. TRT needs a stateful TRT system between the communicating peers, just like NAT systems, and a transport layer connection goes through one particular TRT system, so it can be considered a single point of failure, again like NAT systems. Some other mechanisms, such as SIIT, use stateless translator systems which can avoid a single point of failure. Special code is also necessary to relay NAT-unfriendly protocols, and some of those, including IPsec, cannot be used across a TRT system.

The memo assumes that traffic is initiated by an IPv6-only host destined to an IPv4-only host, and says it can be extended to handle the opposite direction if an appropriate address mapping mechanism is introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator sits between the two worlds and carries the traffic itself instead of rewriting the addresses in each packet. That is why neither end has to be modified, and why the fragmentation problems that come with rewriting headers do not arise.

sections.title: The Transport Relay Technique
sections.content:
The transport relay technique is not new; it has been used in many firewall-related products. TCP relay systems have been used to achieve two goals: disallow forwarding of IP packets across a system, and allow {TCP,UDP} traffic to go through the system indirectly. In the diagram the relay system does not forward IP packets across the inner network to the outer network or the reverse; it only relays TCP traffic on a specific port from the inner network to the outer network and back.

When the initiating host, whose IP address is A, tries to make a TCP connection to the destination host X, TCP packets are routed toward the relay system based on a routing decision. The relay system receives and accepts the packets even though it does not own the destination IP address X. It pretends to have IP address X and establishes a TCP connection with the initiating host as X. It then makes another TCP connection from Y to X, and relays traffic from A to X and the other way around.

Two TCP connections are therefore established: from A to the relay system acting as X, with the addresses on the IPv4 header going from A to X, and from the relay system acting as Y to the destination host X, with the addresses going from Y to X. The relay system needs to capture TCP packets that are not destined to its address; how it does that is implementation dependent and outside the scope of the memo.

For UDP, if you can recognize the inbound and outbound traffic pair in some way, a UDP relay can be implemented in a similar manner. An implementation can recognize the pair as NAT systems do, by recording address and port pairs onto a table and managing table entries with timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: The technique comes from firewalls that let selected connections through without forwarding the packets themselves. The middle system pretends to be the far end for the first connection and opens a second one to the real destination, then copies bytes between them.

sections.title: The Translator and Its Address Mapping
sections.content:
For address mapping, the memo reserves an IPv6 prefix referred to as C6::/64. It should be part of the IPv6 unicast address space assigned to the site, and routing information must be configured so that packets to C6::/64 are routed towards the TRT system. The subnet marked as a dummy prefix does not actually exist.

When the initiating host, whose IPv6 address is A6, wishes to make a connection to the destination host, whose IPv4 address is X4, it needs to make a TCP/IPv6 connection towards C6::X4. If C6::/64 equals fec0:0:0:1::/64 and X4 equals 10.1.1.1, the destination address to be used is fec0:0:0:1::10.1.1.1. The packet is routed towards the TRT system and captured by it. The TRT system accepts the TCP/IPv6 connection between A6 and C6::X4 and communicates with the initiating host using TCP/IPv6. It then investigates the lowermost 32 bits of the destination address to get the real IPv4 destination X4, makes a TCP/IPv4 connection from Y4 to X4, and forwards traffic across the two connections.

There are two TCP connections: one in IPv6 from A6 to the TRT system as C6::X4, with the addresses on the IPv6 header going from A6 to C6::X4, and one in IPv4 from the TRT system as Y4 to the destination host X4, with the addresses going from Y4 to X4.

An initiating host must use this special form of IPv6 address to reach an IPv4 destination host, and the memo says the form can be resolved from a hostname by a static address mapping table on the initiating host, like /etc/hosts in UNIX, by a special DNS server implementation, or by a modified DNS resolver implementation on the initiating host.
sections.plainLanguage: The client is told to address the IPv4 server through a reserved IPv6 prefix: the prefix followed by the server's IPv4 address. The translator reads the last four bytes of that address, learns which IPv4 server is really wanted, and opens the IPv4 connection to it.

sections.title: Notes to Implementers
sections.content:
TRT for UDP must take care of path MTU issues on the UDP and IPv6 side. Because no IP layer packets are relayed between IPv4 and IPv6, the IPv6 path MTU can be decided independently of IPv4 traffic. A simple solution is to always fragment packets from the TRT system to the UDP and IPv6 side to the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1280 octets, which eliminates the need for IPv6 path MTU discovery.

Although the TRT system only relays {TCP,UDP} traffic, it needs to check ICMPv6 packets destined to C6::X4 as well, so that it can recognize path MTU discovery messages and other notifications between A6 and C6::X4. When forwarding TCP traffic, a TRT system needs to handle urgent data carefully. To relay NAT-unfriendly protocols, a TRT system may need to modify data content, just like any translator which modifies IP addresses.

Scalability must be considered carefully when deploying TRT systems to a large IPv6 site. The scalability parameters are the number of connections the operating system kernel can accept, the number of connections a userland process can forward, which equals the number of file handles per process, and the number of transport relaying processes on a TRT system. Design decisions must be made about the proper number of userland processes to support the proper number of connections.

To make TRT for TCP more scalable in a large site, multiple TRT systems can be used. The steps are to configure multiple TRT systems, configure a different dummy prefix for each of them, and let the initiating host pick a dummy prefix randomly for load balancing. That last step can be implemented by installing a special DNS server in the site, configuring DNS servers differently to return different dummy prefixes and telling initiating hosts of different DNS servers, or letting the DNS server pick a dummy prefix randomly. Load balancing is possible because the destination address, and therefore the TRT system, does not change once a TCP connection is established. For address mapping the authors recommend a special DNS server for large-scale installation and static mapping for small-scale installation, since it is not always possible to have a special resolver on the initiating host and assuming it would cause deployment problems.
sections.plainLanguage: For UDP, the translator should simply split outgoing packets to the smallest size IPv6 allows, which removes the need for path MTU discovery. It also has to watch ICMPv6 messages and handle TCP urgent data correctly. A large site should run several translators with different prefixes and let the client pick one at random.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.content:
Combined with a special DNS server implementation, which translates IPv4 addresses into IPv6, TRT systems support IPv6-to-IPv4 translation very well. It requires no change to existing IPv6 clients nor IPv4 servers, so the TRT system can be installed very easily into existing IPv6-capable networks.

IPv4-to-IPv6 translation is much harder to support with any of the translator techniques. While it is possible to use a TRT system for it, it requires nontrivial mapping between DNS names and temporary IPv4 addresses, as presented in the NAT-PT RFC.

TRT systems use the transport layer relay technique to translate IPv6 traffic to IPv4 traffic, which gives two major benefits: the implementation of the TRT system can be done very simple, and the path MTU discovery issue is easier to deal with, because the IPv6 path MTU can be decided independently of the IPv4 path MTU. Even with that simplicity the TRT system can cover most of the daily applications, namely HTTP, SMTP, SSH and many other protocols. For NAT-unfriendly protocols a TRT system may need to modify data content, just like any translator or NAT. And because the TRT system resides in the transport layer, it is not possible for it to translate protocols that are not known to it.

Users normally do not want to translate DNS query and reply traffic using the TRT system. It makes more sense to run a standard DNS server, or a special DNS server that helps the TRT system, somewhere in the site's IPv6 network. There are two reasons. On transport, it is a lot easier to provide a recursive DNS server accessible via IPv6 than to translate DNS queries and replies across the TRT system; putting C6::X into /etc/resolv.conf, where C6 is the TRT reserved prefix and X is the IPv4 address of a DNS server, is rather more complicated than people normally want. On payload, in some installations it makes more sense to transmit queries and replies unmodified across the TRT system, and in others it makes more sense to translate IPv4 DNS queries, such as queries for AAAA records, into queries for A records and back, to invite the traffic into the TRT system. It depends on the installation and configuration at the user's site.
sections.plainLanguage: With a DNS server that hands out the right IPv6 addresses, this works well for the everyday protocols: web, mail and remote shell. DNS lookups are better left outside the translator, and protocols the translator does not know about cannot be carried at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious party may try to use TRT systems like an SMTP open relay for traffic to IPv4 destinations, which is similar to circumventing ingress filtering, or to achieve some other improper use. TRT systems should implement some sort of access control to prevent such improper usage.

A careless TRT implementation may be subject to buffer overflow attack, though that kind of issue is implementation dependent and outside the scope of the memo. Because of the nature of a TCP and UDP relaying service, it is not recommended to use TRT for protocols that use authentication based on the source IP address, such as rsh and rlogin. A transport relay system intercepts a TCP connection between two nodes, which may not be a legitimate behaviour for an IP node, and the memo does not try to claim that it is.

IPsec cannot be used across a relay. And the use of DNS proxies that modify the resource records makes it impossible for the resolver to verify DNSSEC signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator is an open door unless it is restricted, so it needs access control. It breaks any protocol that checks the sender's IP address, and it breaks IPsec altogether. A DNS proxy that rewrites answers also breaks DNSSEC checking.

viz.caption: WHAT THE TRANSLATOR GAINS AND WHAT IT COSTS

items.title: No host changes
items.text: Neither the IPv6 client nor the IPv4 server has to be modified.

items.title: No path MTU problem
items.text: The translator never rewrites an IP header, so it does not have to deal with fragmentation.

items.title: Bidirectional only
items.text: Unidirectional multicast datagrams are not supported.

items.title: Stateful
items.text: Each connection passes through one translator, which is a single point of failure, like a NAT.

items.title: No IPsec
items.text: IPsec cannot be used across a relay.

viz.caption: THE TWO CONNECTIONS AS THE MEMO DESCRIBES THEM

data.title: Connections through a TRT system
data.code:
TCP/IPv6: the initiating host (A6) --> the TRT system (as C6::X4)
       address on IPv6 header: A6 -> C6::X4
   TCP/IPv4: the TRT system (Y4) --> the destination host (X4)
       address on IPv4 header: Y4 -> X4

viz.caption: THE TWO CONNECTIONS A TRT SYSTEM CARRIES, ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC

messages.label: TCP/IPv6 to C6::X4
messages.note: The client opens an IPv6 connection to the reserved prefix followed by the server's IPv4 address.

messages.label: TCP/IPv6 accepted
messages.note: The translator accepts the connection and talks to the client in IPv6.

messages.label: TCP/IPv4 from Y4 to X4
messages.note: The translator reads the lowermost 32 bits of the destination and opens an IPv4 connection to the real server.

messages.label: TCP/IPv4 data
messages.note: The server replies on the IPv4 connection.

messages.label: Forwarded data
messages.note: The bytes are copied across the two connections.
